summary: Sets out terminology, an abstract framework and goals for content negotiation that does not depend on any one protocol. It also identifies technical issues needing more work. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: When you order a meal, the waiter figures out what you can eat. This describes a general way for computers to agree on the best version of something to send.

questions: what is a feature set in content negotiation
subtitle: The vocabulary, abstract model and goals for letting any protocol agree on the best form of a resource to send.

tldr.problem: Many application protocols need content negotiation, but MIME media types cover only one axis of variation, and resources also differ in ways current MIME headers cannot express.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines terms, an abstract framework in which sender and receiver exchange negotiation metadata until a variant is chosen, a list of goals, and open technical issues, without specifying the negotiation process itself.
tldr.outcome: It is a scoping and requirements document: it sets out what a protocol-independent negotiation mechanism should look like and what needs more work, including security risks.

today: RFC 2703 is an Informational memo from September 1999 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It frames the problem and the goals rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Several Internet application protocols need content negotiation for the resources they handle. MIME media types (RFC 2045 and RFC 2046) deal with one major axis of variation, but resources also vary in ways that current MIME headers cannot express.

RFC 2703 sets out terminology, a framework and goals for protocol-independent content negotiation, and points out technical issues. It does not specify the negotiation process. It only indicates the anticipated scope and form of any such specification, and the goals avoid assuming what form the framework will take.
sections.eli5: Websites, email and fax all need to pick the right version of a thing to send. This memo is a plan for a shared way to do that, not the finished machine.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The memo defines a shared vocabulary, many terms adapted from Transparent Content Negotiation (RFC 2295). A negotiable resource is a data resource with multiple representations, called variants. Negotiation metadata is what sender and receiver exchange to decide which variant to transfer.

A media feature is information about the facilities assumed for rendering content, and a feature set describes the full set of attributes a sender, receiver or file can handle. A feature tag names a feature.

Two reply shapes are defined. A choice message returns a selected variant together with the variant list, while a list message sends only the variant list, for when the sender does not want to or may not send a variant. Transmissions can be receiver-initiated ('pull', such as an HTTP GET) or sender-initiated ('push', such as sending email), and modes include connected, session and store and forward.
sections.eli5: A variant is one version of something, like the same story in English or Spanish. Feature tags are the labels that say which version is which.

sections.title: The Abstract Framework
sections.content:
Content negotiation covers three elements: expressing the capabilities of the sender and the data resource, expressing the capabilities of a receiver in advance, and a protocol by which capabilities are exchanged. The framework separates the abstract negotiation process and abstract metadata from concrete representations and protocol bindings, so that it stays independent of any application protocol. Transmission protocol capabilities are explicitly disregarded.

The negotiation is a series of metadata exchanges between sender and receiver that continues until one party determines a specific data file to send. If the sender decides, it sends the file directly. Otherwise the receiver tells the sender its choice. Not every implementation is expected to be this general: TCN, fax negotiation and MIME multipart/alternative are each described as subsets of the process.

The metadata model needs media features, feature sets, naming schemes backed by registration, data types for feature values, a way to combine features into sets with dependencies (for example 640x480 pixels with 256 colours, or 800x600 with 16 colours), and a way to rank feature sets by preference. The memo also suggests a text representation for text-based protocols such as HTTP and SMTP, an ASN.1 description for protocols such as X.400, X.500, LDAP and SNMP, and guidelines for protocol bindings.
sections.eli5: The sender and receiver keep trading notes about what they can handle until one of them can say, 'Let us use this one.' The notes are the same no matter whether they are chatting by web, email or fax.

sections.title: Goals for a Negotiation Mechanism
sections.content:
The goals come in two groups. The generic ones ask for a common vocabulary for features and feature sets, a stable reference for common features, an extensible framework, a way to indicate quality or preference, and a way to capture dependencies between feature values. Negotiation should work efficiently for both pull and push transfers and stand independently of any message transfer protocol.

The protocol-specific goals include that a negotiation should generally identify a mutually acceptable form of data, that capability assertions say who they apply to and how long they are valid, and that negotiation have minimal impact on bandwidth and round trips. Systems should protect users' profiles and providers' inventories of variants, and erroneous capability data must not significantly jeopardize any system. Intelligent gateways, proxies and caches should be allowed to take part, negotiation metadata should be treated as cacheable, and automatic negotiation should not pre-empt a user's ability to choose a format.
sections.eli5: The goals are a wish list: keep it simple and quick, let new things be added later, keep private details private, and still let the person choose in the end.

sections.title: Open Technical Issues
sections.content:
The memo lists questions it leaves open. Does a message-based approach extend to streamed data, interactive computations or real-time acquisition? Should negotiation be end-to-end, which gives the greatest confidence in the outcome, or hop-by-hop, which may suit occasionally connected systems but may need time-to-live and re-verification mechanisms? Third parties, such as an LDAP directory, supplying metadata add chances for error, and using LDAP may need new schema elements such as an attribute type for a media feature set.

It also raises billing (who pays for return messages in a non-connected setting like email or fax), performance, and confidence levels. On performance, multipart/alternative in email saves latency by spending bandwidth, while the HTTP agent-driven negotiation saves bandwidth by adding a round trip. A suggested pattern, taken from TCN, is an optimized procedure that is checked so its result always matches the full negotiation procedure.
sections.eli5: Some puzzles are not solved yet, such as what to do when a movie is still being made while it is being sent, or who pays for the extra messages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo catalogues issues that negotiation protocols should consider. Privacy can suffer from unintended disclosure of personal information and from spoofed requests that only gather data. Denial of service can come from false negotiation data or excessive requests. Negotiating with final recipients through a mailing list clashes with the practice of keeping subscribers' identities confidential.

Protocols that use security services for message transfer should apply them to negotiation too: authenticated requests, authenticated metadata, encryption, and running the exchange over an authenticated or encrypted session such as SASL, TLS or IPSEC. Disclosure of capabilities can reveal which agent is in use, help target macro viruses, or expose less able users who rely on specific content formats. If security features themselves are negotiated, the procedure must not be subvertible to block effective security.
sections.eli5: Telling everyone what your computer can do could help sneaky people. So the notes should be checked, locked up when needed, and not handed out to strangers.

items.title: Media features
items.text: A way to describe attributes of a data resource.

items.title: Feature sets
items.text: Ranges of feature combinations a sender offers, a format represents or a receiver can process.

items.title: Naming and registration
items.text: Names for features and feature sets, with registration to keep them unique.

items.title: Value types
items.text: A framework of data types for media feature values.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text: A way to combine features and express dependencies between them.

items.title: Ranking
items.text: A way to rank feature sets by sender and receiver preference.
